[[File:LeBron James, 25 November 2023 02 (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|[[LeBron James]] was selected to start in the [[NBA All-Star Game]] 22 consecutive times, an NBA record.]]
The [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) [[NBA All-Star Game|All-Star Game]] is an annual exhibition [[basketball]] game. It is the main event of the [[NBA All-Star Weekend]]. Traditionally, the All-Star Game featured a conference-based format, featuring a team composed of all of the top ranked basketball players in the [[Eastern Conference (NBA)|Eastern Conference]] and another team of all-stars from the [[Western Conference (NBA)|Western Conference]]. From [[2018 NBA All-Star Game|2018]] to [[2023 NBA All-Star Game|2023]], the NBA employed a different format featuring two teams captained by the top leading vote-getter from each conference. For the [[2025 NBA All-Star Game|2025 game]], a tournament-based format was used, featuring three teams composed of NBA All-Stars, and a fourth team represented by a mix of NBA rookies, sophomores and [[NBA G League]] standouts that won the [[Rising Stars Challenge]].{{ref label|Note5|e|e}} The [[2026 NBA All-Star Game|2026 game]] will feature a tournament, but with two teams consisting of "U.S." All-Stars and one "World" All-Star team. Following the selection of the all-star starters and reserves, the captains choose from a pool of all-stars to form their teams regardless of conference. Twelve players—five [[Starting lineup|starters]] and seven [[wikt:reserve|reserves]]—from each conference are chosen from what used to be a pool of 120 players—60 players from each conference with 24 [[Basketball positions#Guards|guards]] and 24 frontcourts ([[Basketball positions#Frontcourt (forwards and center)|forwards and centers]])—listed on the ballots by a panel of sport writers and broadcasters to all active players. The starters are chosen by a combination of fans, media, and current players. Fans may vote using a variety of online platforms, and account for 50% of the vote, with the media and current players each accounting for 25%.<ref>{{cite web |title=NBA makes major changes to All-Star voting format |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nba/2016/12/19/nba-all-star-2017-voting-change/95606848/ |publisher=USA Today |date=December 19, 2016 |access-date=January 22, 2017 |archive-date=May 29, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230529003740/https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nba/2016/12/19/nba-all-star-2017-voting-change/95606848/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The reserves are chosen by voting among the [[head coach]]es of each team's particular conference. Coaches are not allowed to vote for their own players, and can select two guards, three front court players, and two players regardless of positions.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/allstar2007/news/story?id=2751331 |title=Anthony snubbed when All-Star reserves announced |access-date=December 24, 2008 |date=February 17, 2007 |work=ESPN.com |archive-date=October 25, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121025154719/http://sports.espn.go.com/nba/allstar2007/news/story?id=2751331 |url-status=live }}</ref> If a player is unable to participate due to injury, the [[National Basketball Association#Presidents and commissioners|NBA commissioner]] will select a replacement.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/allstar2008/news/story?id=3244900 |title=Boston's Allen named All-Star replacement for Washington's Butler |access-date=December 24, 2008 |date=February 13, 2008 |work=ESPN.com |archive-date=December 27, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151227044126/http://sports.espn.go.com/nba/allstar2008/news/story?id=3244900 |url-status=live }}</ref> The league canceled the 1999 All-Star Game due to the [[1998–99 NBA lockout|lockout]].<ref name="lockout">{{Cite web |url=http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/c/a/1998/12/09/SP102770.DTL |title=NBA Drops All-Stars – What's Left? February game in Philly latest casualty of lockout |access-date=December 17, 2008 |work=San Francisco Chronicle |publisher=Hearst Communications Inc |date=December 9, 1998 |first=David |last=Steele |archive-date=September 18, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110918015307/http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=%2Fc%2Fa%2F1998%2F12%2F09%2FSP102770.DTL |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== List ==
The following is a list of players who have been selected for the NBA All-Star Game at least once in their career.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/all%E2%80%93star%5B2%5D |title=all-star |access-date=December 28, 2008 |publisher=Merriam-Webster Online Dictionary |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304055918/http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/all%E2%80%93star%5B2%5D |url-status=live }}</ref> Note that the number indicates the player's number of selections—not the number of games played. For instance, [[Michael Jordan]] was named to the All-Star Game roster 15 times, but missed the 1986 game due to injury.<ref name="jordan">{{Cite web |url=http://www.nba.com/history/players/jordan_bio.html |title=Michael Jordan Bio|access-date=July 3, 2008 |publisher=Turner Sports Interactive, Inc |work=NBA.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902114359/http://www.nba.com/history/players/jordan_bio.html|archive-date=September 2, 2006|url-status=dead}}</ref> As of February 12, 2026, 466 players have been selected to an All-Star Game roster at least once. Of these, 322 of them have earned multiple selections to the game.<!--Both are correct as of February 12, 2026. -->

[[LeBron James]] holds the record for most All-Star Game selections (22), most consecutive selections (22), most games played (20), and most consecutive games played (20). [[Kareem Abdul-Jabbar]] is second in overall selections with 19. [[Kobe Bryant]] is second in consecutive selections with 17. [[Bob Cousy]] and [[John Havlicek]] are tied for second most consecutive games played, appearing in 13 straight All-Star Games. [[Tim Duncan]] also played in 13 straight All-Star Games if the lockout-cancelled 1999 game is excluded; he also owns the record for the most All-Star Games played without missing a game. Several players were named to All-Star Game rosters, but never actually played in the game due to injury.

At age 19, Kobe Bryant was the youngest All-Star selected when he made his All-Star Game debut in [[1998 NBA All-Star Game|1998]], as well as the only player under 20 years old to be selected. Three players have been named NBA All-Stars after turning 40 years old: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, [[Dirk Nowitzki]], and LeBron James. Abdul-Jabbar and James were selected to multiple All-Star Games after turning 40, each with two selections. [[Nathaniel Clifton]] in [[1957 NBA All-Star Game|1957]] was the oldest player to be selected to his first All-Star Game, at 34 years and 3 months old. [[Sam Cassell]] ([[2004 NBA All-Star Game|2004]]) and [[Anthony Mason (basketball)|Anthony Mason]] ([[2001 NBA All-Star Game|2001]]) were the only other players aged 34 or older to be selected to their first All-Star Game.

There have been 45 rookies who were named NBA All-Stars. However, in the [[NBA draft lottery|draft lottery era]] (since [[1985 NBA draft|1985]]), the number of rookies selected to All-Star rosters became even rarer, with only eight rookies selected since, and none with at least two rookies in a game. The [[1985 NBA All-Star Game]] was the most recent game to feature two rookies, with Michael Jordan and [[Hakeem Olajuwon]] being selected. [[Blake Griffin]] in [[2011 NBA All-Star Game|2011]] is the most recent rookie to be named an All-Star, and [[Yao Ming]] in [[2003 NBA All-Star Game|2003]] is the most recent rookie to start in an All-Star Game.

== Notes and references ==
;Notes
*{{note label|Note1|a|a}} Before the 1971–72 season, Lew Alcindor changed his name to Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.<ref name="kareem">{{Cite web |url=http://www.nba.com/history/players/abduljabbar_bio.html |title=Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Bio |access-date=July 3, 2008 |publisher=Turner Sports Interactive, Inc |work=NBA.com |archive-date=February 24, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160224224523/http://www.nba.com/history/players/abduljabbar_bio.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He missed the 1973 All-Star Game for personal reasons.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=940DE0D91F3AF934A15752C0A96E948260 |title=Sports People; 17 Times an All-Star|access-date=December 26, 2008 |work=The New York Times |date=January 27, 1988}}</ref>
*{{note label|Note2|b|b}} When Hakeem Olajuwon arrived in the United States, the University of Houston incorrectly spelled his first name "Akeem". Olajuwon used that spelling until March 9, 1991, when he announced that he would add an H.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nba.com/playerfile/hakeem_olajuwon/bio.html |title=Hakeem Olajuwon Bio: 1992–93 |access-date=June 15, 2008 |publisher=Turner Sports Interactive, Inc |work=NBA.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080516203041/http://www.nba.com/playerfile/hakeem_olajuwon/bio.html |archive-date=May 16, 2008}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |first=Chris |last=Dufresne |title=Hakeem Still Can Be Called 'the Dream' |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |page=2 |date=March 11, 1991}}</ref>
*{{note label|Note3|c|c}} This column does not include [[American Basketball Association]] (ABA) All-Star Game selections.
*{{note label|Note4|d|d}} Before the 2011–12 season, Ron Artest changed his name to Metta World Peace.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nba.com/playerfile/metta_world_peace/bio.html |title=Metta World Peace|access-date=February 10, 2012 |publisher=Turner Sports Interactive, Inc |work=NBA.com|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120211110703/http://www.nba.com/playerfile/metta_world_peace/bio.html|archive-date=February 11, 2012}}</ref>
*{{note label|Note5|e|e}} The list excludes [[Rising Stars Challenge#Past games and rosters|players from the Rising Stars Challenge]] who competed in the All-Star Game tournament, as they are not officially considered NBA All-Stars.
*{{note label|Note6|f|f}} Although Tim Duncan was born in the U.S. Virgin Islands and is a United States citizen,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/virgin-islands/ |title=Virgin Islands |access-date=August 12, 2008 |publisher=[[CIA World Factbook]] |archive-date=January 13, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210113025648/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/virgin-islands/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> the NBA considers him an [[international NBA player|international player]].
*{{note label|Note7|g|g}} Kyrie Irving, who was born in Australia, was raised in America, and has played for the USA Basketball National Team.
*{{note label|Note8|h|h}} Dominique Wilkins, who was born in Paris, settled down in America, and has played for the USA Basketball National Team.
*{{note label|Note9|i|i}} Steve Nash, who was born in South Africa, was raised in Canada.
*{{note label|Note10|j|j}} Tony Parker was born in Belgium. He holds French citizenship and plays for [[France national basketball team|their national team]].
*{{note label|Note11|k|k}} Luol Deng, who was born in Sudan (now South Sudan), was raised in Great Britain, became a naturalized British citizen, and represented England and Great Britain internationally.
*{{note label|Note12|l|l}} Nikola Vučević, who was born in Switzerland, was raised in Belgium and represents Montenegro internationally.
